messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel, a 21-year-old European American man, had been working as a social ministry worker in a war zone when the event that still organized his days occurred: one afternoon, while he was helping distribute supplies near a crowded street, shouting in Arabic rose abruptly over the noise and a group of men in military clothing moved quickly through the crowd. In the crush, the scene turned chaotic and he felt trapped in the middle of it, with the sound of military talk, raised voices, and sudden movement collapsing together into a moment that he now described as impossible to place firmly in the past. Since returning home to his wife, he has found that any conversation about the military, any discussion of what happened overseas, or even hearing Arabic shouted in the distance can pull him back into that afternoon with force. He becomes tense almost immediately, and because those reminders bring up the whole experience, he often stays up very late to avoid the quieter hours when he knows the images and feelings are most likely to come back. He also avoids situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful, because relief feels dangerous to him now, as if letting himself relax would invite the memory to return more vividly.

When Daniel thinks about the event, he says it feels unreal, “too extreme to have actually happened to me,” and yet remembering it brings back the same terror he felt in the moment, with his body reacting before his mind can tell himself he is safe. That terror has fed a persistent sense of threat in ordinary life: strangers approaching him on the street leave him feeling immediately threatened, sudden movements by other people put him on guard at once, and he wakes during the night to check whether he is safe. Those fears are not confined to memory; they shape how he moves through the world, scanning faces and hands, bracing when someone comes too close, and looking toward exits without fully meaning to. The memory itself also seems to intensify the triggers around him, because once he is flooded by the image of that street and the surge of shouting, the slightest military reference or a burst of Arabic can become unbearable again, as if the reminder and the recollection are feeding each other. Even when nothing in his present environment is objectively dangerous, he experiences the world as if danger might arrive from any direction.

He has come to believe that he should have prevented what happened, and he spends long stretches ruminating over every decision, replaying routes, timing, and choices in an effort to find the moment he failed. That searching does not settle him; instead, it keeps the scene active and emotionally close, making the memory feel less like something that is over and more like something still unfolding. The more he remains caught in that review, the more the terror seems to sharpen, and the more on edge he becomes. Because he fears the memory will surge back if he lets his guard drop, he keeps himself busy late into the night and pulls away from anything that might lift his mood or make him hopeful. On difficult days at work, even a casual mention of military activity or the sound of Arabic voices from a neighboring building can send him straight back into vigilance, and then he is once again watching strangers, startled by quick gestures, and trying not to think about the night checks that have become routine.

Over the months, this pattern has narrowed his life with his wife and made his work feel heavier, because he is tired in the mornings and less present around other people. What finally brought Daniel in was that he could no longer keep up the pretense that the fear was passing; he was exhausted by the late nights, the checking, and the sense that one reminder could undo him. He wants help because he is afraid that his world will keep shrinking until he cannot trust ordinary people or ordinary sounds, and because some part of him still hopes he can learn to remember what happened without feeling as though it is happening all over again.
